claims.text: Increasing phosphorus by approximately 2 at% above baseline will improve glass-forming ability.
Increasing phosphorus by approximately 2 at% above baseline will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The proposed baseline phosphorus concentration is approximately 5 at%, and the modified concentration is approximately 7 at%.
Rapid melt quenching of the baseline alloy results in an amorphous structure.
The phosphorus increase should be tested while holding the other elements and processing conditions constant.
The intervention is expected to work when phosphorus is homogeneously distributed and does not form secondary phases.
Increasing phosphorus will produce more extensive phosphorus–transition-metal bonding.
More extensive phosphorus–transition-metal bonding will increase local topological and chemical disorder.
The increased local disorder will reduce atomic mobility and suppress long-range crystallographic ordering.
Added phosphorus will enhance local short-range order, potentially through phosphorus-centered clusters.
Added phosphorus will lower the free-energy difference between the amorphous phase and competing crystalline phases.
Enhanced local short-range order will retard crystal nucleation.
The phosphorus-enhanced alloy will have a larger supercooled-liquid-region width, Tx − Tg, than the baseline alloy.
The phosphorus-enhanced alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation than the baseline alloy.
A larger Tx − Tg indicates increased thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
A lower critical cooling rate indicates enhanced glass-forming ability.
If phosphorus segregation or crystalline phosphorus-rich compounds form above a threshold concentration, the intervention may fail or become detrimental.
The optimal phosphorus increment and the magnitudes of the changes in Tx − Tg and critical cooling rate depend on the specific alloy system.

contradictions.description: Raising phosphorus from about 5 at% to about 7 at% cannot literally leave the atomic percentages of all other elements constant because the total must remain 100 at%. The intended control may be constant relative ratios among the non-phosphorus elements, but this is not stated.
